title: The Phrase By Which He Placed Him At Her Disposal: Mnester, the Dance, and the Order He Could Not Refuse
years: fl. 37-48 CE (birthplace, birth date, parentage and legal status all unrecorded; executed at Rome in 48 CE)
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Rome, a Greek name and nothing behind it
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction from silence, and the date is arbitrary. No ancient source gives Mnester's birthplace, birth year, parents, or legal status at birth; the three writers who preserve him, Suetonius, Tacitus and Cassius Dio, are all silent on every one of those points. A birth horizon in the early first century CE is inference only. Canonical Rome pin, inherited byte-identical from bathyllus_of_alexandria.journey.json and pylades_of_cilicia.journey.json.
stops.campa: Mnester is a Greek word, and it is very nearly all the record gives. No source names his birthplace, his parents, his birth year, or whether he was born free. The three writers who preserve him all begin with him already famous, already at the center of an emperor's attention, as though he had walked onto the page from nowhere. The name belongs to the eastern Mediterranean, which proves nothing: it fits an eastern birth, a slave dealer's choice, or a stage name a dancer picked for himself and kept. Modern prosopography leaves his legal status at birth open, and supplies no year.
suggested_refs: Prosopographia Imperii Romani, second edition, M 646, which leaves his status open
sources: Suetonius, Tacitus and Cassius Dio, silence in all three on origins
Prosopographia Imperii Romani 2, M 646, cited secondhand and not independently consulted

stops.name: Rome, Theatre of Pompey: the Italian dance he inherits
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The art's Augustan foundation by Pylades of Cilicia and Bathyllus of Alexandria is attested; Mnester's personal connection to their school is not. No ancient source links him to either man, to Hylas, or to any named teacher. The date is arbitrary and set inside his working life to order the segment. Theatre of Pompey pin inherited byte-identical from pylades_of_cilicia.journey.json, bathyllus_of_alexandria.journey.json and hylas.journey.json, where it is the corpus's standing pin for pantomime; Dio and Suetonius name no venue for any Mnester performance.
stops.campa: The art he practices is two generations old when he takes it up. Pylades of Cilicia and Bathyllus of Alexandria built it under Augustus out of older dances: one masked dancer carrying every part of a story in his body, while pipes and a chorus supply the words he is forbidden to speak. Hylas, Pylades's own pupil, was dividing Rome into partisans before Mnester was born. Mnester is what that house produces next. Some fifteen years after his death Seneca writes that the house of Pylades and Bathyllus still stands through its successors, and that these arts have many pupils and many teachers.
stops.quote: Stat per successores Pyladis et Bathylli domus, harum artium multi discipuli sunt multique doctores.
stops.quote_source: Seneca the Younger, Naturales Quaestiones 7.32.3 (Latin, thelatinlibrary.com), written some fifteen years after Mnester's death
suggested_refs: E. J. Jory, 'The Literary Evidence for the Beginnings of Imperial Pantomime,' Bulletin of the Institute of Classical Studies 28 (1981)
sources: Seneca, Naturales Quaestiones 7.32.3, Latin verified at thelatinlibrary.com via bathyllus_of_alexandria.journey.json

stops.name: Rome, a freedman of that name on a stone
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and unverified. CIL VI 20139 = ILS 5181 is reported to record a dedication by the Senate and People of Rome to Ti(berius) Iulius Aug(usti) l(ibertus) Mnester. The identification with the dancer recurs in older reference literature and is treated as uncertain by modern prosopography. The inscription's text, findspot and present location could not be checked for this file: db.edcs.eu returned a TLS certificate error and the redirect target was not queried. The date is arbitrary.
stops.campa: An inscription catalogued as CIL VI 20139 records a dedication by the Senate and People of Rome to Tiberius Iulius Mnester, freedman of the emperor. Older reference works identify this man with the dancer, which would make him a freedman of Tiberius and the holder of a public honour granted to almost no performer in the city's history. Modern prosopography leaves the question open and does not close it either way. The stone could not be checked against an epigraphic database for this file, and no findspot appears in anything that was reachable.

stops.name: Rome, no debut on record
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Nothing survives of Mnester's training or early career; the inference that his rise predates 37 CE rests only on Suetonius, Caligula 36.1 and 55.1, whose earliest datable notices already presuppose an established star. The date is arbitrary and set to close the segment. Canonical Rome pin; no specific site is named for this period by any source.
stops.campa: Nothing survives of how he learned. No teacher, no troupe, no first patron, no festival prize, no year in which the city first heard the name spoken. The earliest datable notice already assumes a star, because an emperor does not rebuild the discipline of a theatre around an unknown. So the rise happens somewhere before the year 37, in a city crowded with stages and competing companies, and leaves not one line behind it. Whatever the apprenticeship was, it is gone, and the first thing anyone writes down about him is who he is sleeping with.
suggested_refs: Suetonius, Caligula 36.1 and 55.1, the earliest datable notices, both presupposing an established career
sources: Argument from silence across Suetonius, Tacitus and Cassius Dio

segments.name: Gaius, and the Silence Enforced by Whip

stops.name: Rome, Palatine: named among the emperor's own
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a report, not as an event. Suetonius, Caligula 36.1, explicitly frames the sexual claim as what was said, not as fact; the A tag covers Suetonius making the report. The date is the accession year, set to open the segment; Suetonius gives no date. Note the standing correction: the Latin names Marcus Lepidus and the pantomime Mnester as two separate persons, not one man called 'Marcus Lepidus Mnester'. Palatine pin inherited byte-identical from pylades_of_cilicia.journey.json and hylas.journey.json.
stops.campa: Suetonius, listing what was said of Gaius, sets down three items in a row: Marcus Lepidus, the pantomime Mnester, certain hostages. The Latin gives a comma where later readers will give none, and the senator and the dancer are two men. Suetonius vouches for none of it; he writes that it is said. What the sentence does fix is the company Mnester keeps by the year 37, named in one breath with an Aemilius Lepidus, inside a catalogue assembled to disgrace an emperor. He has no father in the sentence and no city. The Latin runs M. Lepidum, Mnesterem pantomimum, quosdam obsides.
stops.quote: He is said to have had unnatural relations with Marcus Lepidus, the pantomimic actor Mnester, and certain hostages.
stops.quote_source: Suetonius, Divus Caligula 36.1, tr. J. C. Rolfe, Loeb Classical Library (1913)
suggested_refs: Suetonius, Caligula 36.1, Latin: 'M. Lepidum, Mnesterem pantomimum, quosdam obsides'
sources: Suetonius, Caligula 36.1, Loeb 1913, penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Rome, the kiss and the lash
stops.date_confidence: Attested as behaviour, unlocated. Suetonius, Caligula 55.1 says 'inter spectacula', during the shows, and names no building and no single occasion; it describes a habit across the reign. Earlier drafts placed this at the temporary Palatine theatre of the Ludi Palatini, which imports the venue of the January 41 assassination games into a passage that does not have one; the canonical city-level Rome pin is used instead. The date is arbitrary within 37-41 CE.
stops.campa: Gaius kisses him during the shows, in front of the city. And when Mnester dances, silence is enforced with a whip: anyone who makes the smallest sound is dragged out of his seat and beaten, by the emperor's own hand, in the middle of the audience. The price of a cough during a pantomime is a flogging administered by the head of state, and the favour and the violence arrive as one gesture. Suetonius names no theatre and no single day. His phrase is inter spectacula, during the shows, which describes a habit kept up across a reign rather than an occasion.
stops.quote: He used to kiss Mnester, an actor of pantomimes, even in the theatre, and if anyone made even the slightest sound while his favourite was dancing, he had him dragged from his seat and scourged him with his own hand.
stops.quote_source: Suetonius, Divus Caligula 55.1, tr. J. C. Rolfe, Loeb Classical Library (1913)
suggested_refs: Suetonius, Caligula 55.1, Latin: 'ac si qui saltante eo vel leviter obstreperet, detrahi iussum manu sua flagellabat'
sources: Suetonius, Caligula 55.1, Loeb 1913, penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Rome, Palatine: what the charge is made of
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, evidentiary rather than biographical. Suetonius, Caligula 36.1 reports the sexual claim as rumour. The observation that Roman invective habitually weaponized allegations of sexual passivity against subordinate or dangerous men is standard scholarship, not an ancient statement; it neither confirms nor refutes the report. Date arbitrary, set to order the segment. Palatine pin inherited.
stops.campa: Roman invective keeps a standing weapon for men who are dangerous or dependent, and the weapon is the accusation of having been used. Mnester is a performer, legally infamis, barred from the honours of a citizen; he is close to an emperor whom the senate will spend a century blackening. The report of stuprum with Gaius fits that machinery exactly, which is not the same as being false. It only means the record cannot be read as testimony. Whether the thing reported also happened, nothing that survives allows anyone to say.
suggested_refs: Jane Bellemore, 'Gaius the Pantomime,' Antichthon 28 (1994), pp. 65-79, on Gaius's theatrical self-presentation as a target of elite hostility
sources: Suetonius, Caligula 36.1 (reported allegation)
Cambridge Core record for Bellemore, 'Gaius the Pantomime', doi 10.1017/S0066477400000873; the article itself is paywalled and was not read

stops.name: Rome, Palatine: the tragedy Neoptolemus danced
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Suetonius, Caligula 57.4 places the performance at the Palatine games shortly before the assassination; the Latin is verified verbatim ('et pantomimus Mnester tragoediam saltavit, quam olim Neoptolemus tragoedus ludis, quibus rex Macedonum Philippus occisus est, egerat'). Suetonius names no play; the identification as Cinyras is later editorial tradition. Correction carried: the Sulla of 57.2 is 'Sulla mathematicus', an astrologer answering a consultation about Gaius's own horoscope, not a soothsayer volunteering a warning. The exact day is not given; 20 January is set to precede the murder.
stops.campa: Sulla the astrologer, consulted about the emperor's own horoscope, answers that certain death is at hand. Among the signs Suetonius gathers afterwards is this one: at the Palatine games Mnester dances a tragedy that the tragic actor Neoptolemus had performed, generations earlier, at the festival where Philip of Macedon was killed. Suetonius does not name the play. He does not say Gaius was struck down during the performance. He sets the two festivals beside each other, in a list of portents assembled after the fact. The assassination follows within a few days.
stops.quote: The pantomimic actor Mnester danced a tragedy which the tragedian Neoptolemus had acted years before during the games at which Philip king of the Macedonians was assassinated.
stops.quote_source: Suetonius, Divus Caligula 57.4, tr. J. C. Rolfe, Loeb Classical Library (1913); Latin confirmed at lexundria.com/suet_cal/57/r
suggested_refs: The temporary wooden theatre of the Ludi Palatini, January 41 CE
sources: Suetonius, Caligula 57.2 and 57.4, Loeb 1913, penelope.uchicago.edu
lexundria.com/suet_cal/57/r for the Latin

stops.name: Rome, Palatine: the covered passage
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Suetonius, Caligula 58 places the murder in the covered passage the emperor had to pass through on leaving the Palatine games; the date 24 January 41 CE is fixed across the ancient sources, with Josephus, Antiquities 19 giving the fullest parallel narrative. Mnester is not placed at the murder by any source; the coordinate is for the cryptoporticus, and the precise stretch of passage is not identifiable.
stops.campa: On the twenty-fourth of January the emperor leaves the games and takes a covered walkway toward the palace, and Cassius Chaerea, tribune of a praetorian cohort, and the men with him kill him in it. The theatre where Mnester has just danced is a few steps behind. Nothing in Suetonius, Tacitus or Dio places the dancer at the murder, gives him foreknowledge of it, or records a single question put to him about it afterwards. He is the last performer the emperor watched, and that is the whole of his part in the day.
suggested_refs: The Palatine cryptoporticus, traditional site of the assassination of 24 January 41 CE
sources: Suetonius, Caligula 58
Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 19, parallel narrative

stops.name: Rome, nobody comes for him
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction from silence. No source records any investigation, accusation, exile, confiscation or punishment of Mnester in the aftermath of Gaius's assassination; the survival is inferred from that absence in Suetonius, Tacitus and Cassius Dio alike, not from a positive statement. The date is arbitrary, set a few weeks after the murder.
stops.campa: Every favourite of a murdered emperor waits, in the weeks after, to learn whether the new order counts him as property, as evidence, or as a problem to be solved. For Mnester the record is empty: no interrogation, no exile, no confiscation, no charge, no name on any list. Within three years he will be at the center of the next emperor's household in a way he never was in the old one. How he crossed from one reign to the other, who spoke for him, what he gave up, nobody wrote down.
suggested_refs: The purge of Gaius's circle in the weeks after 24 January 41 CE, in which Mnester's name does not appear
sources: Argument from silence in Suetonius, Tacitus and Cassius Dio

segments.name: The Metal of a Dead Emperor

stops.name: Rome, the coinage melted down
stops.date_confidence: Attested, undated within the year. Cassius Dio 60.22.3 records the senate's decree that all bronze coinage bearing Gaius's likeness be melted down. The year is fixed by the consular heading at 60.22, 'when Gaius Crispus and Titus Statilius were consuls, the former for the second time', that is Passienus Crispus cos. II with T. Statilius Taurus, the ordinary consuls of 44 CE; an earlier reading of 43 is corrected here. Dio says nothing about where the melting was carried out, so the canonical Rome pin is used and the Capitoline mint is named only as an unattested possibility.
stops.campa: The senate hates the dead emperor's memory enough to legislate against his face, and decrees that all bronze coinage stamped with the likeness of Gaius be melted down. It is an act of erasure carried out in metal, coin by coin, across a working currency. Dio records the decree and its outcome in one dry movement, and the outcome is not a new coinage. Where the melting was done he does not say. The mint of the period stood on the Capitoline beside the temple of Juno Moneta, but no ancient text puts this particular bronze there.
stops.quote: They hated the memory of Gaius so much that they decreed that all the bronze coinage which had his likeness stamped upon it should be melted down.
stops.quote_source: Cassius Dio, Roman History 60.22.3, tr. Earnest Cary, Loeb Classical Library (1924)
suggested_refs: The damnatio of Gaius and the recall of his bronze coinage, 44 CE
sources: Cassius Dio, Roman History 60.22.3, Loeb 1924, penelope.uchicago.edu
Consular year established from the heading at Dio 60.22

stops.name: Rome, Palatine: promises, then threats
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Cassius Dio 60.22.4, under the consuls of 44 CE. Dio's word is that Messalina was desperately enamoured and could move him neither by promises nor by frightening him. The month is arbitrary; Dio gives no date inside the year. Palatine pin inherited byte-identical from pylades_of_cilicia.journey.json and hylas.journey.json; Dio names no building.
stops.campa: The empress wants him and cannot have him. Dio says she is desperately enamoured, and that neither promises nor frightening him moves him at all. He holds out against the wife of the emperor with no rank, no patron, and no legal standing from which to refuse anything to anyone: he is a performer, legally infamis, and she is the mother of Claudius's children. Four years on, at his trial, the refusal will be the fact that does not save him. Dio does not say how long it lasts, or what the threats were, or who else in the household knew.
stops.quote: She was desperately enamoured of him, and when she found herself unable in any way either by making him promises or by frightening him to persuade him to have intercourse with her, she had a talk with her husband and asked him that the man should be compelled to obey her.
stops.quote_source: Cassius Dio, Roman History 60.22.4, tr. Earnest Cary, Loeb Classical Library (1924)
suggested_refs: Cassius Dio 60.22.4-5, the coercion narrative in full
sources: Cassius Dio, Roman History 60.22.4, Loeb 1924, penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Rome, Palatine: the order that covers him
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Cassius Dio 60.22.5, corroborated in substance by Tacitus, Annals 11.36, where Mnester four years later invokes 'the phrase by which he had placed him at the disposal of Messalina'. Two independent authors preserve the same imperial order, which is unusually strong for anything in this life. Month arbitrary. Earlier notes citing this passage as Dio 60.28 are corrected: 60.28 is the separate later episode, two consular years afterwards.
stops.campa: Blocked, Messalina goes to her husband and asks that the man be compelled to obey her, saying she wants his help for some different purpose. Claudius, told nothing, instructs Mnester to do whatever Messalina orders. The instruction is issued in the open, by the emperor, and it is the emperor who does not know what he has authorized. Mnester lies with her in the belief that this is the thing her husband has commanded him to do. Four years later, in a military camp, he will ask Claudius to remember the exact words.
stops.quote: Claudius accordingly told Mnester to do whatever he should be ordered to do by Messalina; and thus it came about that he lay with her, in the belief that this was the thing he had been commanded to do by her husband.
stops.quote_source: Cassius Dio, Roman History 60.22.5, tr. Earnest Cary, Loeb Classical Library (1924)
suggested_refs: Tacitus, Annals 11.36, where the same order is recalled by Mnester himself in 48 CE
sources: Cassius Dio, Roman History 60.22.5, Loeb 1924, penelope.uchicago.edu
Tacitus, Annals 11.36, Loeb 1937, penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Rome, statues out of the emperor's bronze
stops.date_confidence: Attested as Dio's claim. Cassius Dio 60.22.3-5, consular year 44 CE, states that the recalled bronze became statues of Mnester and that Messalina made them as a thank-offering for his consent. No statue has ever been securely identified, and Dio gives no number, size, or location for them. Month arbitrary. Canonical Rome pin: earlier drafts staged this at the Capitoline mint, which Dio does not support.
stops.campa: The melted coinage does not become a better coin. Messalina takes the bronze that carried Gaius's face and has it cast into statues of Mnester, an offering of thanks, Dio says, for his consent. The dancer who was Gaius's favourite is now standing in Roman metal that was Gaius, put up in public by the woman who had to have him ordered into her bed. Nothing about the statues survives: not their number, not their size, not where they stood, not how long they stood there. No object anywhere has been identified as one of them.
stops.quote: Messalina made statues of Mnester, the actor, out of it. For inasmuch as he had once been on intimate terms with Gaius, she made this offering as a mark of gratitude for his consenting to lie with her.
stops.quote_source: Cassius Dio, Roman History 60.22.3-5, tr. Earnest Cary, Loeb Classical Library (1924)
suggested_refs: The lost bronze statues of Mnester, unrecovered and unidentified in any collection
sources: Cassius Dio, Roman History 60.22.3-5, Loeb 1924, penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Rome, Theatre of Pompey: the stage without him
stops.date_confidence: Attested as an event, reconstructed as a place. Cassius Dio 60.28.3 says only that Messalina took Mnester 'from the theatre' and kept him with her; he names no building. The Theatre of Pompey pin is inherited byte-identical from the corpus's other pantomime files as the standing venue for the art, and is a convention here, not an attestation. Year fixed by the consular heading at 60.28, 'Valerius Asiaticus and Marcus Silanus became consuls, the former for a second time', that is 46 CE; earlier notes giving 44 are corrected.
stops.campa: She takes him out of the theatre and keeps him with her, and the city notices immediately. A pantomime is public property in the way an emperor is: the crowd owns its favourites, argues over them, forms factions and riots for them. Now the best dancer in Rome is simply not dancing, and nobody in authority will say why. Dio names no building. Pompey's is the largest stone theatre in the city and the standing venue for the art, which makes it the likeliest stage for him to have vanished from, and not the recorded one.
suggested_refs: The Theatre of Pompey, principal venue of imperial-era pantomime, unattested for this episode
sources: Cassius Dio, Roman History 60.28.3, Loeb 1924, penelope.uchicago.edu
pylades_of_cilicia.journey.json, bathyllus_of_alexandria.journey.json and hylas.journey.json for the pin

stops.name: Rome, Palatine: the emperor swears he is not in the house
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Cassius Dio 60.28.3-4, consular year 46 CE, quoted verbatim in the Loeb. Month arbitrary. The Palatine pin is inherited; Dio names the palace as the place Mnester is being kept but no room or wing, and does not say where the oath was sworn.
stops.campa: When the talk about Mnester's absence reaches him, Claudius appears surprised. He makes various apologies. He swears that the man is not at his house. The oath is sworn by the same emperor whose standing order put the dancer where he now is, and it is presumably true in whatever sense Claudius understands it and false in every sense that matters to anyone else in Rome. Whether he had forgotten what he authorized two years earlier, or never understood what he had authorized, Dio does not say.
stops.quote: They were also vexed because she had taken Mnester from the theatre and was keeping him with her; but whenever there was any talk among the people about Mnester's failure to dance, Claudius would appear surprised.
stops.quote_source: Cassius Dio, Roman History 60.28.3-4, tr. Earnest Cary, Loeb Classical Library (1924)
suggested_refs: Cassius Dio 60.28.3-6, the whole episode of Mnester's withdrawal from the stage
sources: Cassius Dio, Roman History 60.28.3-4, Loeb 1924, penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Rome, Theatre of Pompey: abed with Orestes
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a line, reconstructed as a place. Cassius Dio 60.28.5 has Mnester put his head out from behind the stage and deliver the line when the crowd clamoured for a particular piece, which fixes the setting as a theatre and not, as an earlier draft had it, the imperial palace. Dio names no specific theatre; the Theatre of Pompey pin is the corpus convention, inherited byte-identical. Month arbitrary.
stops.campa: He does perform, at least once, and the crowd calls for a piece he does not intend to give them. He puts his head out from behind the stage and answers that he cannot comply, he is abed with Orestes. It is a dancer's joke about a role, since Orestes is a part in the repertoire, and it is the only sentence in his own voice that anyone wrote down. The theatre laughs. Whether the people in it hear the second meaning that Dio's readers, a century and a half later, were certainly meant to hear, no source says.
stops.quote: I cannot comply, for I am abed with Orestes.
stops.quote_source: Cassius Dio, Roman History 60.28.5, tr. Earnest Cary, Loeb Classical Library (1924)
suggested_refs: Cassius Dio 60.28.5, the only recorded utterance of Mnester's own
sources: Cassius Dio, Roman History 60.28.5, Loeb 1924, penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Rome, the one man who does not know
stops.date_confidence: Attested in part, glossed in part, and the two are separated here. Dio 60.28.3-6 has the people grieved to think that Claudius alone failed to realize what was going on in the palace; that much is verbatim in the retrieved Loeb text. The further motive circulating in secondary summaries, that the crowd concealed the truth partly from fear of Messalina and partly to shield Mnester, and that they valued him for his beauty, is not in the passage checked and is marked as a gloss. Month arbitrary within 46 CE.
stops.campa: Dio says the people were grieved to think that Claudius alone failed to realize what was going on in his own palace. The city knows. The household knows. The emperor is told nothing and asks nothing, and the arrangement holds for two years. Secondary summaries add that the crowd hid the truth partly from fear of the empress and partly to protect the dancer himself. That motive is not in the text checked for this file, and its origin was not located. It is set down here as somebody's gloss, and not as Dio.
suggested_refs: Cassius Dio 60.28.3-6, and the popular reaction to Mnester's disappearance from the stage
sources: Cassius Dio, Roman History 60.28.3-6, Loeb 1924, penelope.uchicago.edu
The 'fear and protection' motive: source not located, flagged as a gloss

stops.name: Rome, the house lent to them
stops.date_confidence: Attested, and stronger than earlier notes allowed. Tacitus, Annals 11.4 does not merely relay an allegation: he states that the real cause of the brothers' destruction was that they had lent their house for the meetings of Mnester and Poppaea, and calls the formal indictment a pretext. The address is unrecorded, so the canonical city-level Rome pin is used. Month arbitrary within 47 CE.
stops.campa: Two Roman knights of the first rank, brothers, surnamed Petra, are prosecuted and put to death. Tacitus is blunt about the reason: the real cause of their destruction was that they had lent their house for the meetings of Mnester and Poppaea. Not an allegation, in his telling, but the thing underneath the trial. The address is not recorded and no house in Rome has ever been attached to it. The brothers are executed for the loan of a room. Neither Mnester nor Poppaea is charged with anything in these proceedings.
stops.quote: The cause of death lay in the allegation that they had lent their house as a trysting-place for Mnester and Poppaea.
stops.quote_source: Tacitus, Annals 11.4, tr. John Jackson, Loeb Classical Library (1937)
suggested_refs: Tacitus, Annals 11.4, on the prosecution of the two knights surnamed Petra, 47 CE
sources: Tacitus, Annals 11.4, Loeb 1937, penelope.uchicago.edu
Church-Brodribb translation via Perseus, for the 'real cause' wording

stops.name: Rome, the dream of the garland
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Tacitus, Annals 11.4 gives the vision of the night as the actual charge against one of the brothers: Claudius crowned with a garland of wheat turned downward, read as a failure of the grain supply. A variant tradition makes it a white vine-wreath. Month arbitrary within 47 CE; canonical Rome pin, no site given.
stops.campa: The indictment cannot say what the prosecution is actually for, so it says something else. One of the brothers is charged with a dream. He had seen Claudius wearing a garland of wheat with the ears turned downward, and had read from it a failure of the coming harvest. A variant makes the wreath a white vine. Tacitus records the charge and the pretext in the same breath, and does not pretend the court was deceived by either. A man is condemned for the direction the ears of wheat were facing in his sleep.
suggested_refs: Tacitus, Annals 11.4, the dream charge and its variant readings
sources: Tacitus, Annals 11.4, Loeb 1937 and Church-Brodribb via Perseus

stops.name: Rome, Poppaea driven to her death
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Tacitus, Annals 11.1-4 places the suicide of Poppaea Sabina the Elder in 47 CE, inside Messalina's campaign against her and against Decimus Valerius Asiaticus, whose Gardens of Lucullus the empress wanted. Month arbitrary. Canonical Rome pin: the gardens lay on the Pincian, but Tacitus does not place the death there.
stops.campa: Poppaea Sabina, the elder of the two women who carried that name, is driven to take her own life in the same year, inside Messalina's campaign against her and against Decimus Valerius Asiaticus, whose gardens on the Pincian hill the empress wants. The whole affair is a property dispute conducted by capital charges. Mnester's name sits in the middle of it as a cause of death for other people. He is not summoned, not accused, and not asked, on any surviving page, what he did or did not do with her.
suggested_refs: The Gardens of Lucullus on the Pincian, object of Messalina's campaign against Valerius Asiaticus
sources: Tacitus, Annals 11.1-4, Loeb 1937, penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Rome, whether it happened at all
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Nothing outside Tacitus, Annals 11.4 attests any relationship between Mnester and Poppaea Sabina the Elder, and Tacitus is a hostile source writing sixty years later; that he states the meetings as fact makes the report strong, not independent. The reading that the pairing was a prosecutorial convenience within the Asiaticus campaign is inference from the surrounding narrative. Date arbitrary, set to close the segment.
stops.campa: Nothing outside Tacitus attests an affair between Mnester and Poppaea Sabina the Elder. Tacitus states the meetings as fact and calls the dream charge a pretext, which is a strong report from a careful and hostile writer working sixty years after the event. It is also the exact shape a useful fabrication would take inside a campaign whose real object was Asiaticus and his gardens. Both readings survive the evidence intact. Whatever happened in the Petra house, no court ever tested it, and the men who could have been questioned were dead.
suggested_refs: Tacitus, Annals 11.1-4, read as a single campaign narrative rather than four separate prosecutions
sources: Tacitus, Annals 11.4 and surrounding narrative, Loeb 1937

segments.name: The Camp, and the Phrase He Asks the Emperor to Remember

stops.name: Rome, the wedding while the emperor is at Ostia
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Tacitus, Annals 11.26-27, with a parallel in Cassius Dio, records Messalina's public marriage to the consul designate Gaius Silius in 48 CE while Claudius was at Ostia; Tacitus interrupts his own narrative to insist he is not inventing it. The month is arbitrary within the year. No source places Mnester at the ceremony; the stop is at the canonical Rome pin because the household he belongs to is in Rome, not because he is attested present.
stops.campa: With Claudius away at Ostia, Messalina goes through a public marriage ceremony with the consul designate Gaius Silius: contract, witnesses, sacrifice, a wedding feast held openly in the city. It is either a coup or a recklessness so complete that Tacitus stops his own narrative to swear he has invented nothing. No source places Mnester at the ceremony, and none says where he was that day. He belongs to the household the ceremony belongs to. That is the whole of the connection, and it will be enough.
suggested_refs: Tacitus, Annals 11.26-27, the marriage of Messalina and Silius
sources: Tacitus, Annals 11.26-27, Loeb 1937
Cassius Dio, parallel narrative of 48 CE

stops.name: Rome, Castra Praetoria: Silius asks for speed
stops.date_confidence: Attested as event, arbitrary as date. Tacitus, Annals 11.35, quoted verbatim in the Loeb. Tacitus gives no calendar date for the tribunal; October 48 CE is the conventional placement and the days assigned across this segment are ordering devices only. Coordinates corrected: the Castra Praetoria stood at 41.9059, 12.5060, not at the 41.9083, 12.5136 used in earlier notes, which falls some 640 metres north-east, outside the later Aurelian line.
stops.campa: Narcissus, a freedman, organizes the suppression that the emperor is incapable of organizing himself, and moves the business out to the praetorian camp where the swords are. Silius is set before the tribunal, attempts neither defence nor delay, and asks for an acceleration of death. He is consul designate, the second man in the ceremony that started this, and he is granted the one thing he requests. The tribunal then moves to the next name on the list.
stops.quote: Set before the tribunal, Silius attempted neither defence nor delay, and asked for an acceleration of death.
stops.quote_source: Tacitus, Annals 11.35, tr. John Jackson, Loeb Classical Library (1937)
suggested_refs: The Castra Praetoria, whose walls were later absorbed into the Aurelian circuit
sources: Tacitus, Annals 11.35, Loeb 1937, penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Rome, Castra Praetoria: the list of the condemned
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Tacitus, Annals 11.35 names Titius Proculus, Vettius Valens, Pompeius Urbicus, Saufeius Trogus, Decrius Calpurnianus, Sulpicius Rufus and the senator Juncus Vergilianus as condemned with Silius. Mnester is not in that chapter: his case is at 11.36, and earlier notes citing 11.35 alone for his condemnation are corrected. Day arbitrary.
stops.campa: Titius Proculus, Vettius Valens, Pompeius Urbicus, Saufeius Trogus, Decrius Calpurnianus, Sulpicius Rufus, Juncus Vergilianus: knights, officers, a prefect of the watch, a senator. Tacitus sets the names down in a run with the sentence attached to each, the way a clerk reads out a docket. Every man on it has a rank the record can name: knights, officers, a prefect of the watch, a senator. Mnester is not on it. His case comes in the chapter after, at Annals 11.36, and it is the one Tacitus slows down for.
suggested_refs: Tacitus, Annals 11.35, the roll of those condemned with Silius
sources: Tacitus, Annals 11.35, Loeb 1937, penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Rome, Castra Praetoria: the marks of the lash
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Tacitus, Annals 11.36, quoted verbatim in the Loeb. The scars, the torn garments and the appeal to Claudius's own phrase are all in the text; the reader is left to decide whether the lash marks are Messalina's or Gaius's, since Tacitus does not say who inflicted them. Day arbitrary.
stops.campa: He tears his clothes open in front of the emperor. Look at the imprints of the lash, he says, and remember the phrase by which you placed me at Messalina's disposal. The scars are his evidence and his sentence is his charge: he is asking Claudius to recognize four-year-old words, spoken in ignorance, as the instrument that has put him in this room among the condemned. Tacitus, who is not sentimental about performers, records that of everyone brought before the tribunal that day only Mnester made the emperor hesitate.
stops.quote: Only Mnester caused some hesitation, as, tearing his garments, he called to Claudius to look at the imprints of the lash and remember the phrase by which he had placed him at the disposal of Messalina.
stops.quote_source: Tacitus, Annals 11.36, tr. John Jackson, Loeb Classical Library (1937)
suggested_refs: Tacitus, Annals 11.36, the whole of Mnester's hearing
sources: Tacitus, Annals 11.36, Loeb 1937, penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Rome, Castra Praetoria: others from hope, he from need
stops.date_confidence: Attested as reported speech. Tacitus, Annals 11.36 gives the argument in indirect discourse, which means the words are Tacitus's and the reasoning is attributed to Mnester; there is no transcript. Day arbitrary.
stops.campa: The argument he makes is a distinction between two kinds of guilt, and he makes it in a military camp with no advocate and no standing to speak at all. The others wanted something out of Silius. He wanted nothing, and stood to lose more than any of them by the success of the plot he is charged with joining. Tacitus gives the plea in indirect discourse, so the words are his own and the reasoning is Mnester's: others had sinned through a bounty of high hope, he from need, and no man would have had to perish sooner, if Silius gained the empire.
stops.quote: Others had sinned through a bounty of high hope; he, from need; and no man would have had to perish sooner, if Silius gained the empire.
stops.quote_source: Tacitus, Annals 11.36, tr. John Jackson, Loeb Classical Library (1937)
suggested_refs: Tacitus, Annals 11.36, Mnester's plea of compulsion in indirect discourse
sources: Tacitus, Annals 11.36, Loeb 1937, penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Rome, Castra Praetoria: the Caesar leans to mercy
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Tacitus, Annals 11.36: the Caesar was affected and leaned to mercy. Tacitus gives no interval, no deliberation and no report of what Claudius said; the whole of the emperor's hesitation is one clause. Day arbitrary.
stops.campa: It works. Tacitus writes that the Caesar was affected and leaned to mercy, and for the length of one clause the machinery of the day stops on a plea from a performer. What Claudius is being asked to do is admit, aloud, in his own praetorian camp, in front of the men who have spent the day killing senators for him, that he signed the order himself. He is willing to do it. Tacitus records the hesitation and nothing around it: no interval, no deliberation, not one word from the emperor.
suggested_refs: Tacitus, Annals 11.36, on Claudius's hesitation
sources: Tacitus, Annals 11.36, Loeb 1937, penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Rome, Castra Praetoria: the freedmen decide him
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Tacitus, Annals 11.36, quoted verbatim; the freedmen's argument and Mnester's death are both inside that chapter, and earlier notes citing 11.36-37 overreach. Tacitus records no method, no site within the camp, and no words from Mnester after this point. Day arbitrary.
stops.campa: The freedmen who ran the suppression will not have it. After so many executions of the great, they tell him, he cannot spare an actor; when the transgression is that heinous it matters nothing whether it was voluntary or enforced. The argument concedes the entirety of Mnester's defence and then rules it beside the point. It is also an argument about rank, made by former slaves, about a man whose rank stood below theirs. Claudius yields. Mnester is executed, and Tacitus gives neither the method nor the day.
stops.quote: The Caesar was affected, and leaned to mercy; but the freedmen decided him, after so many executions of the great, not to spare an actor: when the transgression was so heinous, it mattered nothing whether it was voluntary or enforced.
stops.quote_source: Tacitus, Annals 11.36, tr. John Jackson, Loeb Classical Library (1937)
suggested_refs: Narcissus and the freedmen of Claudius's household, who conducted the purge of 48 CE
sources: Tacitus, Annals 11.36, Loeb 1937, penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Rome, Castra Praetoria: who is let go
stops.date_confidence: Attested, and included as context for Mnester's own hearing rather than as a claim about him. Tacitus, Annals 11.36 records the execution of Traulus Montanus and the acquittal of Suillius Caesoninus, the latter on the ground that his part in the affair had been the reverse of masculine. Day arbitrary.
stops.campa: In the same proceedings Traulus Montanus is put to death and Suillius Caesoninus is spared, the second, Tacitus says, because in the affair his own part had been the reverse of masculine. The tribunal that has just refused to distinguish between what Mnester chose and what was done to him distinguishes very finely indeed here. Whatever standard is being applied that day, compulsion is not part of it. Tacitus sets the two outcomes down in consecutive clauses and reconciles nothing.
suggested_refs: Tacitus, Annals 11.36, the acquittal of Suillius Caesoninus
sources: Tacitus, Annals 11.36, Loeb 1937, penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Rome, no site, no method, no grave
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction from silence. No source records the date, method or site of Mnester's execution, the disposition of his body, a burial, a monument, a wife, children or an estate. Rome is overwhelmingly likely as the place of death but Tacitus does not state it. The date is arbitrary, set just after the purge. This absence is an argument from silence and is tagged as reconstruction, not as an attested fact.
stops.campa: No source records how he was killed, or where, or on what day, or what was done with the body. There is no tomb, no funerary inscription, no monument, no wife, no children, no estate and no heir in any surviving text. The bronze statues, if they were still standing anywhere in the city, are never mentioned again by anyone. Two knights died for lending him a room and their prosecution runs to a full chapter of Tacitus. His own death is the last clause of a sentence about what the freedmen persuaded the emperor to do.
suggested_refs: The absence of any funerary record for Mnester across Tacitus, Suetonius and Cassius Dio
sources: Argument from silence in Tacitus, Annals 11.36-38, Suetonius and Cassius Dio

stops.name: Rome, among the shades that meet Claudius
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a text, disputed in translation and in authorship. The Apocolocyntosis is conventionally assigned to Seneca the Younger, with the attribution debated; composition is usually put shortly after Claudius's death in October 54 CE, and the date here is that year. The Latin was fetched directly at thelatinlibrary.com and is verbatim. The gloss 'made him shorter' is not settled: 'decoris causa minorem fecerat' is commonly read as mutilation or castration for the sake of his looks, and the neutral reading should not be presented as agreed.
stops.campa: Six years after the camp, a satire on the dead Claudius has the emperor arrive among the shades to a crowd of singers, and standing in the middle of them is Mnester the pantomime, whom Claudius had made smaller for the sake of his looks. The Latin is disputed and the polite reading is not the likeliest one: decoris causa minorem fecerat is commonly taken as mutilation rather than height. Whichever way it runs, the joke is that the emperor's welcoming party in the underworld is assembled entirely from his own victims.
stops.quote: Medius erat in hac cantantium turba Mnester pantomimus, quem Claudius decoris causa minorem fecerat.
stops.quote_source: Seneca (attributed), Apocolocyntosis divi Claudii 13, Latin text via thelatinlibrary.com
suggested_refs: Apocolocyntosis 13, and the philological dispute over 'decoris causa minorem fecerat'
sources: Seneca (attributed), Apocolocyntosis 13, thelatinlibrary.com/sen/sen.apoc.shtml, fetched directly
No verbatim English Loeb rendering was retrieved for comparison

stops.name: Florence, the single witness
stops.date_confidence: Attested as manuscript history, arbitrary as a date, and not a place Mnester ever went. Annals 11-16 survive through one codex, the Second Medicean, written in the eleventh century and now Plut. 68.2 in the Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana at Florence. The date 1500 orders the segment and marks the codex's Florentine period, not its copying. Coordinate corrected to the Laurentian library in the cloister of San Lorenzo, 43.774521, 11.253374; an earlier note gave the Piazza del Duomo, some 570 metres south-east.
stops.campa: Everything Tacitus preserves of him comes down through one book. The torn garments, the scars, the plea, the freedmen's argument: the whole hearing survives in a single eleventh-century manuscript, the Second Medicean, written at Monte Cassino and now shelved as Plut. 68.2 in the Laurentian library at Florence. Had that codex burned, Mnester would be a man Suetonius says an emperor kissed and Dio says was cast in bronze, with nothing at all said in his own defence. There is no second copy anywhere to check the text against.
suggested_refs: Florence, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Plut. 68.2, the Second Medicean codex of Tacitus
sources: Standard manuscript tradition of Tacitus, Annals 11-16
Wikipedia, 'Laurentian Library', for the building's coordinates

stops.name: Rome, the comma that made two men one
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a translation, corrected as to source. The fused name is demonstrably carried by the Bohn / Thomson English Suetonius, which renders Caligula 36 as 'inflamed with an unnatural passion for Marcus Lepidus Mnester, an actor in pantomimes', against Latin reading 'M. Lepidum, Mnesterem pantomimum, quosdam obsides'. The attribution of the error to Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities (1875) could not be confirmed: penelope.uchicago.edu refused connection on four attempts, and Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography entry 'Mnester' carries no fused name. The 1855 date is approximate for the Bohn edition.
stops.campa: Suetonius wrote M. Lepidum, Mnesterem pantomimum, quosdam obsides: three items, two men and a group of hostages. A nineteenth-century English translation dropped the comma and produced an unnatural passion for Marcus Lepidus Mnester, an actor in pantomimes, and the fused name went into circulation as though the dancer had been carrying a senator's praenomen and gens all along. It is the tidiest thing that ever happened to him, and it is not his. Smith's biographical dictionary does not repeat it. English Wikipedia does not repeat it. The Latin has never once said it.
stops.quote: inflamed with an unnatural passion for Marcus Lepidus Mnester, an actor in pantomimes
stops.quote_source: The Lives of the Twelve Caesars, Caligula 36, Bohn / Thomson English translation, via en.wikisource.org
suggested_refs: The Bohn / Thomson English Suetonius, demonstrable carrier of the fused name
sources: en.wikisource.org, 'The Lives of the Twelve Caesars/Caligula'

stops.name: Rome, a birth year invented by a database
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a record. Wikidata Q6885941 gives birth 1 CE, death 48 CE, place of death Rome, and cites the Pauly-Wissowa Realencyclopadie entry 'Mnester 1' as a describing source. The death year is Tacitus; the birth year is a database placeholder with no ancient attestation whatever. The screen-reception credits are carried from the same article and were not independently verified: the Caligula (1979) film page returned HTTP 404 twice this session. Date is the year of consultation.
stops.campa: His modern authority record gives a birth date of 1 CE, a death in 48, place of death Rome. The death is Tacitus. The birth is a placeholder, entered because a database row wants a number in a field where the ancient world supplied none, and it will be copied outward from there in five languages. Screen adaptations do the same work in a different medium. A face is cast, a voice assigned, dialogue written for a man who left exactly one recorded sentence, and the sentence is about being in bed with Orestes.
